lab_title: The Retrograde Puzzle: Why Mars Reverses in the Night Sky
top_level_objectives: Describe apparent retrograde motion as the periodic westward reversal of an outer planet against the background stars over weeks to months
Explain why the geocentric model required epicycles to reproduce retrograde loops and why this was awkward
Demonstrate that the heliocentric model produces retrograde motion naturally through the relative orbital motion of Earth and an outer planet
Connect the relative-motion explanation to an everyday analogy (overtaking cars) and predict how retrograde behavior differs for Jupiter and Saturn

scenes.brief_purpose: Ground students in the raw observation that motivated centuries of astronomical debate, without yet explaining it.
key_visuals: A night sky dome overhead filled with recognizable background constellations
Mars shown as a bright reddish point of light positioned against the stars
A subtle horizon and foreground silhouette to establish the ground-based vantage point
student_actions: Look up and locate Mars among the labeled background constellations
Note and record Mars's starting position relative to a nearby bright star

scenes.brief_purpose: Let students personally discover retrograde motion by advancing time and seeing Mars reverse direction.
key_visuals: A time-lapse control (dial or slider) advancing the sky night by night over several months
Mars leaving a visible trail of past positions that first drifts eastward, then slows, loops westward, and resumes eastward
A date/time readout marking each night's observation
student_actions: Advance the timeline step by step and watch Mars trace its path
Mark on the trail where Mars appears to slow, stop, and reverse
Answer a prompt describing the shape of the loop they observed

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how ancient astronomers preserved an Earth-centered cosmos by inventing epicycles, and let students feel how contrived it is.
key_visuals: A geocentric diagram with Earth fixed at the center and Mars riding a small circle (epicycle) on a larger orbit (deferent)
The epicycle spinning to reproduce the same looping path students saw in the sky
Side-by-side comparison of the epicycle-generated loop with the observed sky trail
student_actions: Manipulate the epicycle to try to match the observed loop
Reflect via a prompt on why adding circles-upon-circles feels unsatisfying as an explanation

scenes.brief_purpose: Reveal the heliocentric arrangement and reframe the problem from a Sun-centered, top-down view.
key_visuals: A top-down view of the Sun at the center with Earth and Mars on their separate, smooth circular orbits
Orbit paths drawn as clean circles with Earth on the faster inner orbit and Mars on the slower outer orbit
Labeled arrows showing each planet's orbital speed and direction
student_actions: Rotate and zoom the solar-system view to inspect both orbits
Compare the orbital speeds and distances of Earth and Mars

scenes.brief_purpose: Deliver the core explanation: the loop is an illusion produced when faster Earth overtakes slower Mars.
key_visuals: Earth and Mars animating along their orbits with sight-lines drawn from Earth through Mars out to the background stars
The projected position of Mars on the distant star field tracing the retrograde loop in real time as Earth passes Mars
A synchronized split view linking the outside orbital motion to the Earth-sky appearance
student_actions: Play the synchronized animation and watch the sight-line sweep backward as Earth overtakes Mars
Identify the exact interval during which Earth passes Mars and match it to the westward loop

scenes.brief_purpose: Cement the relative-motion concept with an intuitive everyday parallel.
key_visuals: Two cars on a highway, a faster car overtaking a slower one in the next lane
The slower car appearing to drift backward against distant background scenery as the faster car passes
A visual mapping showing the fast car as Earth, the slow car as Mars, and the scenery as background stars
student_actions: Trigger the overtaking animation and observe the apparent backward drift
Match each element of the analogy (fast car, slow car, scenery) to its astronomical counterpart

scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the principle to other outer planets and let students predict how distance changes the effect.
key_visuals: Selectable orbits for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn shown at their relative distances from the Sun
Retrograde loops of each planet displayed on the background star field, with Mars's loop largest and Saturn's smallest
A comparison panel summarizing loop size versus orbital distance
student_actions: Switch between Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn to view each planet's retrograde loop
Predict which planet loops least and confirm the prediction using the outside view
Complete a summary prompt explaining why more distant planets produce smaller retrograde loops
